input.quote: 7.2 Before engaging another provider, Customer must disclose and match for Vendor any more favourable commercial offer it receives.
input.rationale: Section 7.2 (the first clause numbered 7.2) conditions our ability to engage any other provider on first disclosing a competing offer and giving Vendor the chance to match it. That is a de facto exclusivity/right-of-first-refusal binding Customer: it restrains our freedom to source elsewhere for the entire term, is not confined to a defined product or service category, has no 12-month limit, and gives no automatic exit on Vendor's failure to meet service levels or delivery dates. It therefore fails the fallback and sits in walk-away territory (exclusive dealing for the full term with no performance-based exit). It also directly conflicts with Section 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges Customer has made no exclusivity or most-favoured-customer commitment. The exclusivity that runs in our favour (e.g. Section 12.3) is untouched. The price-matching/MFN aspect is separately relevant under the MFN rule; here the deletion is driven by the restraint on our sourcing freedom.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have deleted the requirement to disclose and match competing offers before engaging another provider: it operates as an open-ended right of first refusal and de facto exclusivity on us, with no product-category limit, no time limit, and no exit if Cobalt misses service levels. It also contradicts Section 12.3, in which Cobalt acknowledges we have given no exclusivity or most-favoured-customer commitment. If some pre-switch engagement is important to you, we can consider a good-faith notice right limited to a defined service category for twelve months, ending automatically on any service-level failure.
proposal.summary: Delete Section 7.2 disclose-and-match obligation (de facto exclusivity/ROFR on Customer).
